summary: Add CaRT test for singleton attach
description:
Singleton attach is used by CPPR to attach to the local CNSS process.   It stopped working in a recent version of CaRT.

Please add a test for this feature to avoid this problem in the future.   The existing CaRT echo test can actually be used but the line needed is commented out.

In line 169 of crt_echo.h, the flags need to be set to CRT_FLAG_SINGLETON.   
For it to work on the client, CRT_ALLOW_SINGLETON=1 should be set in the environment for both the client and server and the bit should be set on the client in crt_init.   Unfortunately, you don't want to set that bit when you don't want to be treated as a singleton client so the test case can't be checked in without further modification to make that bit setting optional.  One option would be to set the bit if CRT_ALLOW_SINGLETON is set in the environment.

e.g.
if (getenv("CRT_ALLOW_SINGLETON")) flags |= CRT_FLAG_BIT_SINGLETON;

Then a test needs to be added to set that bit.

See CART-109 which has usage.   You run the server with orte and the client without orte.

summary: Rearrange self-test message structures to pack correctly without #pragma pack
description:
Currently the self-test session ID is 4 bytes and is located at the beginning of self-test messages. This means that the following items are misaligned (on an 8-byte boundary) and so a pragma is currently used to force no padding to be inserted. Using a pragma in this way might cause problems later (based on real problems DAOS is having already with similar code). 

To fix this, the session-id needs to be promoted to an 8-byte value.

summary: Applications need a way to keep progressing until the queue is empty
description:
When CaRT does a broadcast, the handler is invoked before reply aggregation occurs.   This is problematic for shutdown RPCs which initiate a shutdown sequence after executing the handler, potentially stopping the progress thread.

The current workaround is to call crt_progress in a loop with a long timeout (e.g. 1 second) and loop until it returns -DER_TIMEDOUT.   This workaround allows the reply aggregation to execute so that a reply gets sent to the parent before the process stops calling crt_progress.   It works fairly well in practice but this same code is duplicated throughout numerous projects and this should be handled in cart.  We either need a way to flush the queue when shutting down or a flag to crt_destroy that does the same.

summary: d_rank_list_copy() is unsafe.
description:
There's a function exported by CaRT but only used in daos to copy rank lists.  The code looks at the length of the source list and copies the list to the dest, without knowing or checking the length of the dest array.

An initial fix is to modify the code so that the copy will only happen if the dest list is bigger than the source list, however this has the effect of truncating the apparent size of the dest group, so it's possible that subsequent copies will fail.

A complete fix would be to ensure that the list size is always correct, which would mean that list_copy() needed to perform an allocation, or to track both array size and current length in d_list_t

summary: Per context default timeouts?
description:
Currently there's a default cart timeout (60 seconds), a environment variable to override this for the entire library, and a function call to change a RPC timeout after it's created but before it's sent.  A API to set the default timeout, either similar to how the environment variable works, or on a per-context or per opcode basis would be useful.

Setting a timeout for every RPC in IOF would be both intrusive and error-prone, and it makes sense that there should be at least an API to mirror the environment variable.

summary: Fix iv_client/iv_server test race
description:
Currently number of CART tests that have both a client and server component have a problem where a server might not be fully started before the client starts and tries to attach to the servers group.

As a workaround, number of tests have a loop in which they attempt to attach (either indefinitely or for retry amount of tries) until successful.

A better solution is needed to ensure server full start before clients are started up. Perhaps a helper function that everyone could use that would block until attach file is created.

 * If no PSRs in the list have responded, retry them in a round-robin manner indefinately

summary: restore the use of OFI_PORT
description:
From: "Li, Wei G" <wei.g.li@intel.com>
To: "Jia, Yulu" <yulu.jia@intel.com>
CC: "Oganezov, Alexander A" <alexander.a.oganezov@intel.com>, "Liu, Xuezhao" <xuezhao.liu@intel.com>
Date: Thu, 30 Aug 2018 18:06:52 -0700
Subject: RE: OFI_PORT

Yes, please.

We'd like a way to specify the URIs before starting DAOS servers. When the servers start, the actual URIs it listens on shall be based deterministically on what we specified. If any of the URI is unavailable, we expect CaRT to give up creating that context. (If no URI is specified, we expect CaRT to select available ones dynamically.)

OFI_PORT seems to satisfy this requirement for sockets, according to cart/README.env. For some other providers, we heard from the OFI team that there will be ways to specify addresses as well, though supporting them in CaRT is not urgent.

Thanks,
liwei

summary: URI tracking changes
description:
Currently each local context stores node-related information as part of the crt_lookup_item structure. This structure contains fields of:

316 /* connected HG addr */
317 hg_addr_t li_tag_addr[CRT_SRV_CONTEXT_NUM];
318 crt_phy_addr_t li_uri[CRT_SRV_CONTEXT_NUM];

where li_tag_dddr is the per-tag uri-string address of the remote node.

and li_tag_addr is an hg_addr_t structure returned from mercury, which (this needs to be verified) for some providers is formed by combination of local and remote tag + address.

 

While li_tag_addr will need to be per-local-and-remote context, the li_uri is only identifying remote targets and does not need to be stored per-local tag/context.

As such this optimization is to change how/where li_uri is stored. Instead of storing it per local context, it is better to store all remote uris in a single table that would be identified as (remote_rank, remote_tag) -> (remote_uri)

 

crt_lookup_item would then be modified to simply point to that global table entry instead of storing it locally.

summary: Use Broadcast for communicating RAS notifications.
description:
the root of the subscribed service processes broadcasts RAS notifications to the entire process set

the broadcast needs to be fault tolerant as well. the next root has to take over if the real root dies


A reminder of how the RAS broadcast needs to work:

# Some ranks are selected to subscribe to RAS notifications.
# RAS subscribers early inject RAS events and put them on a pending queue
# The RAS leader (the subscribed node with the lowest rank) send out a broadcast for each eviction.  The broadcast goes to the process set, however excludes ranks which are on the pending queue.
# The broadcast is retried until success, potentially allowing for more RAS events and therefore longer exclude lists to allow previously failing broadcasts to succeed.
# After a successful broadcast then the RAS leader then broadcasts the next pending eviction on the list.  In this way there is only ever one broadcast on the wire at a time.
# The RAS leader repeats until there are no more pending RAS events on the queue.
# If a subscribed node becomes the RAS leader because it sees a pending event through RAS for all lower-ranked subscribed nodes then it assumes the leadership role and starts broadcasting eviction events, starting with the latest eviction broadcast it itself received.

This is safe because it relies on the following semantics:
* There is only one broadcast in progress at any one time.
* On RAS leader failover a new leader steps in, and replays any event which may not have been globally acknowledged.
* Broadcasts are idempotent on all nodes, as the same eviction broadcast may be received more than once

summary: Add method for verifying pointers used in input structure
description:
We need a method for detection of situations when input rpc structure contains pointers to the fields that are allocated on stack instead of heap. 

When input rpc structure points to anything on stack, it must perform progress (after crt_req_send()) while in the same stack frame, or else garbage data will be copied into input, if crt progress is done asynchronously.

The method for this check does not need to run every time, so it can be non-optimal/hacky and can be enabled manually on demand to ensure we don't have bugs similar to CART-555

summary: Performance analysis of Network stack latency
description:
Need to look at latencies in the network stack and determine a path for performance optimizations. 

Currently CaRT selt test is showing 7 usec latency using PSM2. and ~10usec with Verbs  Need to look at entire networking stack and determine where this time is being spent: ofi, mercury layer, & CaRT.

Johann's expectation is that ofi latencies should be around 1usec and mercury/cart are an additional 6usec (need analysis).

 

Should investigate performance bottlenecks with messaging rates (RPC/sec) in network stack (CaRT/Mercury/OFI/provider).  Start with low level FI ping pong test with OFI, and then do something similar for Mercury & CaRT layers.  Performance analysis of stack (VTune?) to show and prioritize hotspots to investigate.

summary: DSM: hash dkey/akey over service threads
description:
The DSM client should compute a hash over the dkey and akey to select what service thread (i.e. endpoint tag) to send the request to. The actual number of service threads on each target is available through the pool map.
It does mean that, for now, an update/fetch operation with two i/o vectors pointing at two different akey might end up sending two requests over the wire to the same storage server. This can be improved in the future.

summary: go-spdk package should dynamically link libraries on install
description:
h3. Problem statement:

[go-spdk bindings package|https://github.com/daos-stack/go-daos] needs to be able to install/compile without error to enable _"go get_ " to behave as expected, installing _go-spdk_ currently requires linking to libraries that May not exist at package install time which is an issue when retrieving and installing on the builders for CI.

Currently library paths are provided when building _daos_server_ with _scons_ (_daos_m/src/control/Sconsscript_), dynamic linking will enable library detection at Go run-time rather than compile-time enabling package to compile and install even if dependent libraries are missing.
h3. Potential solutions:
 * Using command "_go get -d_" just for this package would work but it's introducing a special case which is not ideal.
 * Integration of the bindings into _daos_ source would remove the need to fetch and install bindings package before prerequisite libraries were built, it would however stop the bindings from being a stand-alone package.
 * Dynamic linking (_dlopen_) to enable package detection at run-time.

h3. Dynamic loading and linking:

Using _cgo_ to link against required libraries directly can only be done at compile time.

_dlopen_ can be used to detect libraries at Go run-time and therefore allow package completion and installation to complete with missing libraries but retrieving library handles and symbol lookup needs to be performed manually (_cgo_ does this for you). _struct_ and other type definitions exported in shared library have to be referenced in header files in advance.

Dynamically loading C libraries from within a Go process to provide capability (for Go application) to compile and install before building required C libraries: 
 - instead of statically linking with cgo, use dlopen (via cgo) to link at runtime with specified list of paths
 - get library handle (exit on failure) and look up required function symbols
 - void pointer cannot be used directly from Go as a function pointer if looked up at runtime (like it can if cgo links at compile time), therefore need to pass to C function (exposed to Go using cgo) which accepts pointer and any arguments to the function, can then cast pointer to appropriate function pointer type and call with supplied arguments (could use [coreos dlopen wrapper|https://github.com/coreos/pkg/blob/master/dlopen/dlopen.go] or just _C.dlsym/dlopen_ directly)
 - C access function needs header definitions for lib signatures ahead of run-time loading/linking to specify function signatures including return struct (type); therefore _nvme_discover.h_ needs to exist in spdk Go dir
 - in order to lookup symbols with _C.dlsym_, C glue code interacting with SPDK needs to be linked against _libspdk.so_ and built into _libnvme_discover.so_ (can be done in scons script or with a go build command)

h3. Other considerations:
 - Plugin / module approach in Go refers to building interfaces with shared libraries built from Go, not from C [https://github.com/vladimirvivien/go-plugin-example]

h3. References:

[https://www.quora.com/Systems-Programming/What-is-the-exact-difference-between-dynamic-loading-and-dynamic-linking/answer/Jeff-Darcy]

summary: Convert Go dependencies from script to vendor directory.
description:
We need a better way to manage our Go dependencies. Currently anyone running a build must call a bash script (utils/fetch_go_packages.sh) to "go get" the dependencies and put them into an appropriate GOPATH for the build.

Vendoring is a common way to manage dependencies in Go. This is the placement of dependency source code in a directory called "vendor" underneath the Go project directory. I.e. $GOPATH/src/projectname/vendor. Go looks in the vendor directory first, then GOPATH/src, then GOROOT/src. This also allows us to pin dependencies at a specific version.

summary: Create mechanism for daos_io_server to listen and respond to incoming dRPC messages
description:
Design and implement the drpc C API to listen for and process messages. This will be leveraged by the daos_io_server.

Assumptions:
 * The drpc listener process will live in its own dedicated Xstream and is permitted to block for (short) periods of time.
 * Shutdown will be handled by detecting a shutdown condition between loop iterations at the caller level.
 * Only one client session at a time, initially. In the future this code could be reused, and may need redesign. For now as long as one client session is supported, it's good.
 * The accept-recv-handle-send loop should be implemented inside a drpc_progress function that can be called with a timeout.

Design and implement the drpc C API to listen for and process messages. This will be leveraged by the daos_io_server.

Assumptions:
 * The drpc listener process will live in its own dedicated Xstream and is permitted to block for (short) periods of time.
 * Shutdown will be handled by detecting a shutdown condition between loop iterations at the caller level.
 * Only one client session at a time, initially. In the future this code could be reused, and may need redesign. For now as long as one client session is supported, it's good.
 * The accept-recv-handle-send loop should be implemented inside a drpc_progress function that can be called with a timeout.

summary: DAOS two-phase commit transaction (DTX)
description:
We have got some agreement about the DAOS transaction model. We will implement DAOS two-phase commit transaction (DT2) to guarantee the data consistency when modify multiple-replicated objects. Be as the first step, it will be server-sonspored. Means that the client sends the modification RPC (UPDATE/PUNCH) to some leader (per-dkey based), then the leader will forward the modification RPC to other non-leaders (please note that the bulk data is transferred between client and servers, not between leader and non-leaders).

The DT2 model will also be used to guarantee the data consistency for other DAOS non-atomic modifications, such as modifying the erasure-coded object.

summary: Create rpc module framework for daos_io_server to handle incoming dRPC messages
description:
Integrate the dRPC listening API from DAOS-1427 into the daos_io_server. The daos_io_server should add an xstream that sets up the dRPC listening socket and kicks off a loop that does the following:
 * Watch the socket for activity (with a timeout)
 * If a client attempts a connection, accept it
 * If a client sends a drpc message on an open connection, handle it and send a response.
 * Check for shutdown condition. If detected, close all open socket fds and clean up, exit.

Add a mechanism to register the drpc module handlers into the daos_io_server, so they can be looked up and called as needed.

summary: Run spdk in multiprocess mode from control plane
description:
In order for multiple processes to interact with the same NVMe device through SPDK, multiprocess mode must be enabled through EAL [https://spdk.io/doc/nvme.html#nvme_multi_process_configuration] .

The situation arises where this is needed when control plane discovers local NVMe controllers and namespaces and subsequently execs a shell command to run burn-in workloads on the device through SPDK and FIO.

Experimentation with running the initial discovery in a Go-routine was performed with the expectation that after the routine completed the relevant resources would be returned to SPDK and the subsequent burn-in would be able to run without multiprocess mode enabled, this experiment was unsuccessful in that the hypothesis proved false. It is likely that some references/context existed in process memory after the execution of the Go-routine that caused the SPDK/FIO process to fail.

summary: Array Value Type VOS Storage
description:
VOS is able to store and retrieve multiple checksums for Array Value types. Storage of the checksums will be in the evt_desc while the checksum metadata (size, type, chunksize) will be in the evt_root. Eventually this meta data will be configured for a container and thus be stored in the container metadata/property.

The chunk size, extent size, and record size will be used to determine the number of checksums needed and the size of the checksum buffer.

Chunks must be aligned to the "chunk size".

Some use cases must be considered:
- Not same written as read must return the correct checksums. For example: written (0-3), (4-7), then read (0-7) or written (0-7), read (0-3).
- Holes in an extent fetched. For example: written (0-3), (8-11), read (0-11)


VOS tests are expanded to verify the value written is read.

summary: run spdk in multi-process mode as secondary for daos_io_server
description:
Currently running multiple _daos_io_server_s on same node is not supported, because each _daos_io_server_ will call _spdk_env_init()_ in ‘primary’ mode and reserve hugepages. In that situation, the first started _daos_io_server_ will use up all the hugepages, and other _daos_io_server_s will fail to get any available hugepages.

To support multiple _daos_io_server_s on same node (and in order to perform discovery while running _daos_io_servers_), SPDK global initialization should be performed in _daos_server_ (including _spdk_env_init()_), configuring multi-process mode so that _daos_server_ runs in ‘primary’ mode and the _daos_io_server_s run in ‘secondary’ mode.

summary: Remove auto/format parameters from server configurations
description:
Consensus reached that given we now have explicit provisioning stages and format is not automated, auto/format parameters should be removed from config.

background context:

--------29/01/19
 Discussion related to DAOS installation/deployment workflow.
 Proposal to support two use cases, a preferred normal flow:- involving initial start-up of daos_server instances- live provisioning through authenticated dmg distributed grpcs
 and a flow more suited to distributed launch environment such as kubernetes:- initial provisioning through one-shot daos_server command mode invocations using distributed launcher capabilities and associated authentication (e.g. pdsh)- delay daos_server startup until provisioning completed

--Use case 1:
 $ # install RPMs & modify config file$ exec -n \{nodes} daos_server –setup-scm-interleaved -f /etc/daos_server.yaml$ exec -n \{nodes} reboot # required for SCM reconfiguration$ # setup daos_server to start automatically through system.d or equivalent$ # start daos_server$ dmg firmware_upgrade -n \{nodes} ...$ dmg burnin -n \{nodes} ...$ dmg format -n \{nodes} ... # --force required on subsequent reformat$ dmg status # too few servers have joined$ dmg status # still too few servers...$ dmg status # all joined!

--Use case 2:
 $ # install RPMs & modify config file$ exec -n \{nodes} daos_server –setup-scm-interleaved -f /etc/daos_server.yaml$ exec -n \{nodes} reboot # required for SCM reconfiguration$ exec -n \{nodes} daos_server –firmware-upgrade -f /etc/daos_server.yaml ...$ exec -n \{nodes} daos_server –burnin -f /etc/daos_server.yaml ...$ exec -n \{nodes} daos_server –format -f /etc/daos_server.yaml ... # --force required on subsequent reformat$ # setup daos_server to start automatically through system.d or equivalent$ # start daos_server$ dmg status # too few servers have joined$ dmg status # still too few servers...$ dmg status # all joined!
----
Proposal to have a read only configuration and pass user-specified parameters either via commandline or user supplied parameter overrides file. server configuration updated by daos_server after processing user supplied parameters.
 Consensus reached on invoking daos_server with sub commands rather than options for one-shot command mode e.g. "daos_server format ...".
 Agreement on need for format state gating so io_server not forked before SCM formatted, the state is to be persisted.
 Question on whether io_servers should be started individually (if one io_server on storage node fails format, should a second be started?)
 Clarification that format stage will require cleaning of nvme devices (do we need to use "nvme reset" or can we use SPDK?)
 Question on whether whitelist/blacklist should exist in server config.
 Assumption that server configurations files will usually be the same across storage server nodes (potentially shared w/ NFS etc) given normally homogenous hardware configurations, but configuration files are per-server allowing flexibility for heterogeneous hardware configurations.
 Consensus reached that given we now have explicit provisioning stages and format is not automated, auto/format parameters should be removed from config.
 Clarification that a system config with persistent parameters should exist.

summary: NVMe test Plan: Pool Capacity (Basic tests)
description:
Purpose: Verify pool & container behavior on SSDs by creating pools & containers that represent various fractions of the overall available SSD capacity. Perform I/O up to the anticipated capacity of the created pools to verify allocated capacity can be used.

Case 1: Create a small pool/container – a few GB. Use IOR to write to the container, just short of the capacity (should work). Continue writing beyond the available capacity (ENOSPC).

Case 2: Create a pool/container that matches available SSD space. Use IOR to write to the container, just short of the full capacity (should work). Continue writing beyond the available capacity (ENOSPC).

Case 3: Perform pool/container create followed by delete; repeat this 100s or 1000s of times. Verify no capacity is leaked over the course of the create/delete cycles.

Case 3: Perform pool/container create followed by delete; repeat this 100s or 1000s of times. Verify no capacity is leaked over the course of the create/delete cycles.

summary: MS151 DAOS ESSIO Stabilization (SOW v1)
description:
MS151        DAOS ESSIO Stabilization

01/01/2018 – 03/30/2019

 
 # The DAOS prototype developed in the Extreme Scale Storage and IO (ESSIO) program provides the core set of functionalities to support future DAOS development.
 # After active development cycles through the ESSIO program, a stabilization effort is required to harden the DAOS prototype.
 # This intense testing and consolidation phase will provide solid foundations for new feature development.
 # The Subcontractor shall stabilize the DAOS prototype delivered in Q2’17 as part of the ESSIO program.
 # This hardening effort consists in consolidating the prototype along two axes:
 ## Addressing the technical debt accumulated through the development cycle
 ## Intensive testing and bug fixing

 # This will result in a version of DAOS that can operate at reasonable scale under heavy workload with robust recovery mechanisms. This milestone will also provide:
 ## A baseline for the DAOS design documentation for regular updates when new future features are added
 ## A first version of the DAOS operations manual with instructions on how to build, install and run DAOS

 

Deliverables

The Subcontractor shall:

(1) provide a report that documents successful completion of the regression test suite and lists the changes that have been addressed in this milestone;

(2) push all changes to the open source branch;

(3) provide a revised DAOS design documentation;

(4) provide an initial version of the DAOS operations manual.

 

This milestone will be considered complete when:

(1) the Subcontractor delivers the report to Argonne;

(2) the Subcontractor presents the report at the quarterly meeting;

(3) the report is considered complete to the reasonable satisfaction of Argonne

summary: Drop privileges before starting io_server
description:
PROBLEM STATEMENT

When started for the first time by root (or with sudo), daos_server enters "maintenance mode" when privileged tasks such as hardware provisioning can be performed. In this mode, requests can be made from the management tool but the data plane service will not be started.

When provisioning is complete, format can be called from the control plane management tool. The format phase prepares and allocates the nonvolatile storage (NVMe/SCM) to be used by the DAOS data plane.

After the format phase, when elevated privileges are no longer required, privileges should be dropped to that of a normal user (user and group name can be supplied in the server configuration file).

Then data plane services will be started owned by non-root user.

 

In summary, the aim is to run the complex data plane (daos_io_server) services as non-root user whilst allowing privileged operations through control plane (daos_server) for hardware provisioning.

 

Previous implementation attempt of changing the ownership of the currently running process (daos_server) after hardware provisioning (format phase) proved unsuccessful due to complications involving SPDK/NVMe access from multiple processes and the inability to release resources during process lifetime.
 - NVMe devices are accessed by daos_server through SPDK, running in primary mode, to provide storage provisioning capability.
 - NVMe devices are accessed by daos_io_server through SPDK, running in secondary mode, to provide storage access to DAOS data plane.
 - It doesn't seem possible (no provided capability) to release SPDK resources within a process lifetime after SPDK environment initialisation.
 - After changing the ownership of the primary SPDK process to a non-root user, NVMe related device files are still owned by root user.
 - Attempting to enable access to the non-root user through the provided spdk scripts/setup.sh fail because the primary SPDK process presumably has open handles to the aforementioned device files.
 - Subsequent spawning of secondary SPDK processes by primary process running as non-root user fail to access NVMe devices.

PROPOSAL

Re-spawn process owned by target non-root user after hardware provisioning rather than changing the ownership of the currently running process. When started initially as root, limited communication services will be made available and only unlocked when run as a normal user.

After maintenance activities complete and format phase succeeds, change ownership of control plane files to new user and spawn shell command.

When re-spawned and process owned by normal user, data plane services will be started owned by normal user.
 - Shell command is fired off and daos_server (root) terminates gracefully.
 - Shell command is of the format "<small delay> && <spdk setup new user> && <daos_server (new user)>"
 - spdk setup completes successfully because root process had terminated and released resources
 - subsequent daos_server (non-root) runs SPDK in primary mode, skips maintenance/format phase, launches all comms (agent/iosrv drpc) and spawns daos_io_server running SPDK in secondary mode.

summary: Enable snapshots within new Epoch model
description: With the new epoch model, aggregation is performed without an explicit "epoch slip" request. This means that snapshot creation must be relayed to all Container targets to prevent it from being aggregated away locally. The idea is that due to limited SCM capacity, the default state on every target is to aggregate continuously as data is written. In order to create a snapshot, the leader sends a first broadcast to all target which suspends the aggregation until snapshot creation is complete and also synchronizes the HLC (Clock) – at this point, the local HLC on each target and the leader indicates the max of all the values collected during the broadcast. A snapshot entry is created for this timestamp and a second broadcast is sent to notify targets that a snapshot has been created and they may resume aggregation. If a leader goes during the process, it must be taken to its conclusion by the newly elected leader.

summary: Replace (or augment) DAOS error codes in debug messages with strings
description:
We print things like rc = -1011 in many places. Gurt has a mechanism for translating these codes (at very little cost) to strings. We should print the strings in our error messages. This would be a good task for someone who is getting familiar with our process.

The plan for the 1st patch is:
 To change all rc printouts to use d_errstr() output for all files under daos/src that use these GURT debug macros: #lines
 . D_INFO
 . D_NOTE
 . D_WARN : 3
 . D_ERROR: 569
 . D_DEBUG: 42
 . D_CRIT    : 4
 . D_FATAL  : 6

The typical code change will look like:
 - D_DEBUG(DF_DSMC, "failed to create container: %d\n", rc);

+ D_DEBUG(DF_DSMC, "failed to create container: %s\n", d_errstr(rc));

The output will be like this:

11/18-21:16:52.91 boro-59 DAOS[52915/52915] container DBUG src/container/cli.c:120 cont_create_complete() failed to create container: DER_NO_HDL

summary: Enable multiple tag specification in ftest.sh
description:
Currently ftest.sh supports passing tags to launch.py if they are specified as a single tag or a comma-separated list which will only run tests that contain all of those tags.  To enable running tests that have either one tag or another the tags must be specified as a space-separated list.  The tags can be passed into ftest.sh as a space-separated list, but the code does not correctly handle $TEST_TAG as a string containing spaces.

The proposed change would:

1) replace any spaces or commas in $TEST_TAG with dashes to enable the variables use in directory paths

2) Pass $TEST_TAG to launch.py without being encapsulated by parenthesis to allow the program to parse the arguments correctly

This will enable pull requests to use CI to run both tests that matched both the "regression" and "vm" tags (the current default) and tests that matched a tag that included the test cases being added or modified in the pull request.

summary: manual: single target exclusion with insufficient capacity for rebuild
description:
*Environment*: Use 1 client, 3 servers for this test.

*Test Steps*:
 * Create one pool on all ranks with one container using RF=2 objects
 * Create a second pool on ranks 0-2 with one container using non-replicated objects
 * Use IOR to fill the container in the first pool to 50% capacity
 * Use IOR to fill the container in the second pool to 90% capacity
 * Fail the third server (rank 2)
 * Verify rebuild fails due to space limitations, the data is still accessible, and the second pool is in a degraded state due to lack of replicas

h2. Manual Test
The requirement says "Proper error is reported via control plane (dmg) if recovery cannot complete due to lack of space on the surviving servers." This means we need to verify the error message obtained from some dmg command. The error message is generated from rebuild failure due to lack of space after killing server rank(s). (I assume "recovery" here refers to rebuild.) We need to verify the error message itself rather than whether the error message appears in certain situation. Thus, this test is to verify the contents of the error message; e.g., whether certain string or error code exists in the message.
h3. Setup
2 hosts. One of them runs 2 server ranks and the other runs 3. 8 targets. tmpfs.
h3. Test Steps
# Start the servers.
# Create a pool of 50GB.
{noformat}
dmg -i --json pool create --scm-size=10GB
{noformat}
# Create a POSIX container with object class SX. SX is supposed to distribute objects across targets, without replication.
{noformat}
daos container create --pool=$POOL --type=POSIX --oclass=SX
{noformat}
# Call pool query and check the leader.
{noformat}
dmg -i pool query --pool=$POOL
{noformat}
# Run ior with SX. Write 50GB or more data. I think we need to have -F for ior.
{noformat}
~/runtime_mpich/bin/mpirun -hostfile ~/mkhostfile -np 50 ~/first_ior/bin/ior -F -a DFS -b 1G -w -W -k -G 1 -o /testfile -t 1M --dfs.chunk_size 1048576 --dfs.cont $CONT --dfs.dir_oclass SX --dfs.group daos_server --dfs.oclass SX --dfs.pool $POOL
{noformat}
It eventually fails with no space left error. It should have filled up to 19GB free space, which means 62% full.
# Stop 2 server ranks so that we reduce the total size by 40%, which means some of the written data will be lost. Stop the non-leader ranks by looking at the pool query output earlier. I'm not sure it matters, but it's better to rule out external factors.
{noformat}
dmg -i system stop --ranks=2,4
{noformat}
# Wait for several seconds and check the server terminal. You should see {{Rebuild [failed]}} repeatedly. When you start to see it, call pool query again and check the rebuild status. It can be failed or busy depending on the timing, so try it until you see failed as below.
{noformat}
[mkano@wolf-3 src]$ dmg -i pool query --pool=$POOL
Pool 46172d32-c8fe-4f0e-975e-4f01423d39e6, ntarget=40, disabled=16, leader=3, version=19
Pool space info:
- Target(VOS) count:24
- SCM:
  Total size: 30 GB
  Free: 12 GB, min:371 MB, max:706 MB, mean:487 MB
- NVMe:
  Total size: 0 B
  Free: 0 B, min:0 B, max:0 B, mean:0 B
Rebuild failed, rc=0, status=-2026
{noformat}
Also check the status is -2026: Data lost or not recoverable (DER_DATA_LOSS), which is what we expect.

h3. Note
The key of this test is to write the amount of data large enough so that stopping server ranks makes the rebuild fail. However, this can be very challenging.

One reason is that I can't fill up the pool above 75% (only 62% in the above steps) and understanding and controlling this number is hard. I talked to several people, created a ticket, and they all say it's possible to fill up above 75%. There are several parts that impact the ability to fill up such as number of ranks, number of targets, size of pool, object class, etc. However, I couldn't figure out the right combination. The object allocation mechanism is just unclear.

Another reason is that we can't kill more than half of the ranks. If we kill half of them, pool query becomes unresponsive. Killing more servers is the alternative to filling up the pool. For now, the test works because we can fill up the pool to 62% and we can kill the ranks to reduce the capacity down to 60%. However, this may not be possible in the future and we may not be able to observe the rebuild failed -2026. In that case, talk to the control plane team to see if we can make the pool query responsive after killing half (or more) ranks.

Also check the status is -2026: Data lost or not recoverable (DER_DATA_LOSS), which is what we expect.

h3. Note
The key of this test is to write the amount of data large enough so that stopping server ranks makes the rebuild fail. However, this can be very challenging.

One reason is that I can't fill up the pool above 75% (only 62% in the above steps) and understanding and controlling this number is hard. I talked to several people, created a ticket, and they all say it's possible to fill up above 75%. There are several parts that impact the ability to fill up such as number of ranks, number of targets, size of pool, object class, etc. However, I couldn't figure out the right combination. The object allocation mechanism is just unclear.

Another reason is that we can't kill more than half of the ranks. If we kill half of them, pool query becomes unresponsive. Killing more servers is the alternative to filling up the pool. For now, the test works because we can fill up the pool to 62% and we can kill the ranks to reduce the capacity down to 60%. However, this may not be possible in the future and we may not be able to observe the rebuild failed -2026. In that case, talk to the control plane team to see if we can make the pool query responsive after killing half (or more) ranks. $acceptance criteria:$

summary: manual: multi-target exclusion with insufficient capacity for rebuild

 * Create one pool on ranks 0-2 with one container using RF=2 objects

 * Fail the third server (rank 2)
 * During rebuild fail the last server (rank 3)
 * Verify the first rebuild succeeds
 * Verify the second rebuild fails due to space limitations, the data is still accessible, and the second pool is in a degraded state due to lack of replicas

summary: Test Automation: IO with Server/System restart Functional test
description:
Environment:

1 server

1 client

Purpose:
 * Verify Pool created and IO on nvme with different pool sizes and different data size with server/system restart

Description: 

(After server start SPDK need to be setup again.)

Case1:
 * Create the Pool with small NVMe size (0/1G/48G)
 * Write/Read data (<4K) 1B/1K/4K
 * Write the data/ Stop Servers/Start Servers/Read data back and check data integrity.

Case 2:
 * Create the Pool with small NVMe size (0/1G/48G)
 * Write/Read data (>4K) 1M/16G
 * Write the data/ Reboot the node/ Start servers/read data back and check data integrity.

Case3:
 * Create the Pool with Maximum NVMe size.
 * Write/Read data (<4K) 1B/1K/4K
 * Write the data/ Stop Server/Start Server/Read data back and check data integrity.
 * Use the maximum pool size based on NVMe size on each server and number of total servers.

Case4:
 * Create the Pool with Maximum NVMe size.
 * Write/Read data (>4K) 1M/16G 
 * Write the data/ Reboot the node/ Start server/read data back and check data integrity.

summary: Enable yaml file host replacement in launch.py for easy manual testing
description:
Provide a mechanism similar to ftest.sh which replaces the boro-[A-H] server/client placeholders in the test yaml files with a specified list of host names to enable easier manual execution of the tests without needing to modify the yaml file to use the reserved servers.

Update launch.py to accept two new command line arguments:

--test_servers, -ts
     A comma-separated list of host names to replace yaml server placeholders

--test_clients, -tc
     A comma-separated list of host names to replace yaml client placeholders

Launch.py will create a copy of the selected test's yaml file and replace the server/client placeholders with the requested host names.  If a yaml file contains more placeholders than are specified by the user the placeholders without replacements will be omitted from the modified yaml file.  Upon completion of the test the modified yaml file should be removed.

summary: Implement system stop/start through control plane
description:
*[https://wiki.hpdd.intel.com/display/DC/DAOS+Tools]*

From the tool syntax specification above this covers "_dmg system stop|start|query_" which are described as:

_stop_: full shutdown of the DAOS service
_start_: restart service after full shutdown

 
h2. Stop - controlled shutdown

Controlled shutdown is ultimately what we are aiming for, organising the graceful termination of necessary services in an orderly manner without triggering rebuild (as would happen in unexpected failure modes).

Shutdown is to be coordinated through the management service access points when a request is received from the management tool. The shutdown will be coordinated as follows:
 # A "dmg system stop" request is sent over gRPC from the management tool to an access point (MS replica).
 # Access point queries membership list of DAOS system (membership populated from join requests on start-up) and sends gRPC "prepare shutdown" requests to membership (fan-out) which results in dRPC calls to each member. "prepare shutdown" dRPC handler executes logic to inhibit pool svc rebuild. This is termed the "first stage" of controlled shutdown.
 # Once "prepare shutdown" requests have returned successfully, another gRPC fan-out to all members is performed, this time to stop the member instances. Fan-out gRPC "stop" requests attempt to "kill rank" over dRPC and resort to OS kill(pid) from daos_server if initial attempt fails. gRPC returns when instances have been stopped.
 ## gRPC requests return error on timeout
 ## members list maybe polled and requests retried accordingly
 ## member requests contain rank identifiers to terminate
 # Access point terminates local instances once all members have returned acknowledgements of instances being terminated.
 # Request from management tool returns (if previously interrupted, management tool can query progress and any failures)

After stopping instances,  _daos_server_ should continue running and listening for requests. Instance metadata, held in the superblock, will be retained.

Further iterations will allow for individual instances to be queried and stopped/restarted individually.

original_description_sprint:

From the tool syntax specification above this covers "_dmg system stop|restart_" which are described as:

_stop_: full shutdown of the DAOS service
 _restart_: restart service after full shutdown

With regard to the task of shutting down a DAOS system, after having discussed with team members I will suggest two proposals. The reason for the two proposals is based around the decision of whether a "controlled shutdown" is practical/feasible or not and whether this is a critical requirement rather than just a complicated nice-to-have.

*We should note that Lustre has chosen not to provide a systemwide shutdown capability.*
h2. Proposal #1: Stop - controlled shutdown

Controlled shutdown is ultimately what we are aiming for, organising the graceful termination of necessary services in an orderly manner without triggering rebuild (as would happen in unexpected failure modes).

Shutdown is to be coordinated through the management service access points when a request is received from the management tool. The shutdown will be coordinated as follows:
 # A request is sent over gRPC from the management tool to an access point.
 # Access point queries membership list of system over dRPC and set management service "stopping" state (which potentially inhibits rebuild)
 # gRPC multicast to all members in list which results in request being sent over dRPC, gRPC returns when instances have been stopped.
 ** gRPC requests return error on timeout
 ** members list maybe polled and requests retried accordingly
 # Access point terminates local instances once all members have returned acknowledgements of local instances being terminated.
 ** if errors returned due to timeouts then failure is reported to management tool
 ** if force flag specified in original request, local instances forcefully terminated, timeouts ignored and global state set regardless
 # Request from management tool returns (if previously interrupted, management tool can query progress and any failures)

After stopping instances,  _daos_server_ should continue running and listening for requests. Instance metadata, held in the superblock, will be retained.

Further iterations will allow for individual instances to be queried and stopped/restarted individually (probably after implementation of "_system query_")

"_system restart_" will cause the harness to start any formatted io_server instances (with intact superblocks) but should not need to send requests over dRPC.

*Unresolved Questions:*

concerns:
 - adverse interactions with D system

*Feature Delivery:*

Only the implementation of the RPC mechanism for triggering the shutdown is targeted for 0.8 release (this ticket) and follow-on tickets will be created for the remaining tasks.

 
h2. Proposal #2: Stop - abrupt shutdown, rebuild inhibited

Controlled shutdown may end up being impractical and less useful than we anticipate due to the complexity required to cover all failure and edge cases.

Alternative approach is for the administrator to terminate the processes (daos_server) either directly or through the control plane management tool after disabling rebuild.
 # Rebuild behaviour inhibited by sending request to management service via access point.
 # daos_server instances will be terminated by sending a suicide request from management tool (host either retrieved from MS system membership or provided directly by admin) starting with all storage servers that are not MS replicas.
 # System membership list can be queried to check progress of shutdown.
 # Once system membership list has been reduced to the list of MS replicas, terminate on those hosts as per step #2.

As no control plane (daos_server) instances will be running after shutdown they would need to be restarted as needed. In order to provide maintenance mode after shutdown it may make sense in this scenario to not start data plane automatically and instead wait for an explicit "system start" command from the management tool.
h2. Proposal #3: Stop - instance shutdown, rebuild inhibited

Slight variation on proposal #2. Instead of terminating control plane (daos_server) services, send instance shutdown requests to each storage server control plane process.

The potential benefit of this proposal is that the control plane will remain active after shutdown (although management service will not be). Restart will involve signalling control plane on each host to bring up configured instances.

 
h2. Proposal Summaries:
 # Access point host orchestrates shutdown through multicast to system members and decides actions based on responses. (least administrative burden, highest complexity)
 # Manual shutdown and restart of control plane processes (most administrative burden, lowest complexity)
 # Trigger IO instance shutdown explicitly on each control plane process but leave control plane running. (medium administrative burden, medium complexity)

summary: Dedicated dRPC listener xstream
description:
Move the dRPC listener thread to its own dedicated xstream in the DAOS IO server.

The new thread is responsible for:
 * Polling and managing the dRPC connections.
 * Receiving incoming messages from the socket.
 * Creating ULTs for the incoming message handlers on the system xstream, as many of these handlers need to call other modules designed to be run only in xstream 0 (rdb, etc.).
 * Processing dRPC completion events and sending the final response to the client.

summary: Validate SCM configuration
description:
Optane NVDIMMs have a number of configurable features. These features are configured/optimized using the DAOS control-plane CLI or by config file. 

*Objective:* Verify the configuration variations on NVDIMM devices and the validity as negative inputs are provided to the configuration.

*Environment:*

This test can be done with a single client & server.

*Test Steps/options:*
 * Configuring devices that have already been configured and are in use by DAOS
 ** Prepare the SCM
 ** Start server with pmem specified in the server config
 ** Verify that if the pmem is already mounted, should return error on storage prepare
 ** If pmem exists and is not mounted, just the details of the existing device will be returned (no change to the device will be made)
 * Configuring devices that are not in a usable state.
 ** Start with no prepared pmem devices
 ** Run (for example) `ipmctl set -dimm 1234 FatalMediaError=1` to inject an error on DIMMs.
 ** Attempt to run storage prepare and verify it does not complete successfully

summary: Standardizing on server/agent yaml file specifications
description:
Even though the launch.py script, and therfore CI, and the daos/src/tests/ftest/util/apricot/apricot/test.py code support different yaml file keys for specifying hosts to run daos_server and daos_agent, it would be ideal to standarize on one per role, e.g. 'test_servers' and 'test_clients'.  It would also be benefitial for all tests specifying servers and agents to inherit the TestWithServers apricot class to utilize the same common code for reading these values from the yaml files. 

To make tests more portable we should explicitly specify hosts (placehoders, e.g. boro-B) in the yaml file for the daos_agent (using the 'test_clients' key) and fail the test - as opposed to using the current host - if one is not specified.  The current host's name can still be specified via the yaml file to run the daos_agent locally.

summary: Use pydaos module conditionally
description:
This is an improvement that may be needed to enhance DAOS-2786

1. Should we conditionally just build pydaos2 or python3?
Currently we build both pydaos_shim_27 or pydaos_shim_3 
in src/client/pydaos/SConscript:
    build_shim_module(py_env, svars, '$PREFIX/lib64/', "2.7")
build_shim_module(py_env, svars, '$PREFIX/lib64/', "3")
 
After discussion with Johann and Phil, they both do need to be built, because even the node that installs DAOS RPM
May only have one active python version running, but that’s a runtime condition we need to check.
In DAOS build time, we need to build pydao_shim for both to make sure it can run on any nodes either 
having python2 or python3.

2. Make sure runtime on the node that install DAOS RPM, only one of the pydaos module be used 
   conditionally match the active python version.

    PYTHONPATH is ftest.sh is already set properly only to include the runtime python version.
    In launch.py, PYTHONPATH will be addressed in DAOS-2759.

3. May be add a README.md in daos/src/client/pydaos?

    DASO-3433 is expanding the Python bridging to DAOS API project started by DAOS-2786, the README.md will be moved from
   its original location src/utils/py to this new directory. Probably better to reuse that existing README.md, update it when this bridging
   project in completion phase.

description:
If prepare NVMe is performed while the server is running (from management tool), scan will not show updated results after prepare (devices will not be shown even though they are accessible to SPDK).

Don't cache and rediscover devices on each scan, overhead is deemed minimal and the benefit of having up-to-date information sufficiently beneficial.

* reboot the servers

summary: daos_server network scan shouldn't require a config
description:
If I run {{daos_server network scan --all}} without a valid server config, I'll get an error complaining that no fabric provider is specified in the config.

From a usability perspective, it would be nicer if that subcommand would supply a valid-enough configuration to successfully run the command and generate output, so that the admin could see what they have on their system before they configure it.

So, if there is already a config and it has fabric stuff set, then that should be preferred as the source of default values. If the loaded config would fail validation due to missing fabric values, then the config should be updated with fabric values that are good enough to pass validation and provide useful results.

summary: DAOS SDL CT203-Security Test for safe handling of invalid structure contents (priority 10)

When processing a data structure from an untrusted source, the contents of that data structure, such as relative offset fields and pointers, are also untrusted data. Verify that malicious or invalid data structures are detected and handled securely:

Test case 1: Modify the pointer addresses to point outside the loaded struct. • A common malware tactic is to manipulate pointer addresses to retrieve malicious code or to obtain sensitive data. •

Test case 2: Insert offset fields or padding (depending on the flavor of data structure) to expand parsed data beyond the maximum allowed size. These are often abbreviated out of headers to save space, but inserted back in during the parsing phase. Additional test cases may be appropriate depending on the characteristics of the implementation you are testing. Consider what unexpected forms the incoming data could take.

[https://sharepoint.amr.ith.intel.com/sites/HPD/Shared%20Documents/A21%20Program/A21%20SDL/SDL%20Tasking/daos-a21-daos-10-release-all-tasks-report.pdf]

When processing a data structure from an untrusted source, the contents of that data structure, such as relative offset fields and pointers, are also untrusted data. Verify that malicious or invalid data structures are detected and handled securely:

Test case 1: Modify the pointer addresses to point outside the loaded struct. • A common malware tactic is to manipulate pointer addresses to retrieve malicious code or to obtain sensitive data. •

Test case 2: Insert offset fields or padding (depending on the flavor of data structure) to expand parsed data beyond the maximum allowed size. These are often abbreviated out of headers to save space, but inserted back in during the parsing phase. Additional test cases may be appropriate depending on the characteristics of the implementation you are testing. Consider what unexpected forms the incoming data could take.

description:

Verify that minimal permissions are configured when opening pipes and ports Note: Name of the interface depends on what programming language and/or framework you are using. It may be a pipe, a port, or a similar construct. Whether externally facing or limited to inter-process communications, opening pipes and ports with unnecessary permissions can provide an opportunity for malicious access or overwrite of privileged data. Do not rely on secure defaults for permissions settings. • Some platforms and frameworks may have insecure defaults if permissions are not configured correctly.

For example, by default an opened port or pipe may inherit the permissions of the process that opened it. • Due to configuration differences, end users may encounter different behavior and/or defaults from what you see on your development/testing systems. • The BKM is to explicitly configure minimal permissions

summary: DAOS SDL CT26 Security Customize Security and Privacy Validation Plan (priority 10)
description:
Details for task can be found by searching CT26 in the document below

[https://sharepoint.amr.ith.intel.com/sites/HPD/Shared%20Documents/A21%20Program/A21%20SDL/SDL%20Tasking/daos-a21-daos-10-release-all-tasks-report.pdf]

Customize Security/Privacy Validation Plan

Security/Privacy Validation Planning is a critical step in ensuring that the security/privacy requirements are validated. A well documented Security/Privacy Validation plan enables reuse downstream by receiving products/platforms and/or next gen product validation teams. For HW, The Security and Privacy Validation Plan is an extension of the Security and Privacy Validation Strategy document already created.

Review Assigned Tasks and other Sources of Requirements SD Elements assigns a set of problems (or threats) and associated testing tasks for the project to address based on the responses to the survey. These problems are the basis for the threat model. For SW, the problems and tasks assigned by the tool may fully address all of the threats and validation needs for the project. It is possible, however, that there are additional threats and validation needs that were not discovered by the survey that require additional exploration. For FW and HW there will definitely be additional threats and validation needs that are not covered by the knowledgebase that will require additional security and privacy validation tasks.

 

Generate a Security/Privacy Validation Plan

If the set of testing tasks assigned to the project already addresses the relevant threats and security/privacy objectives, then the security/privacy validation plan is effectively complete. If, however, additional validation is needed then generate a Security/Privacy validation plan. The validation plan must include:

• A description of in scope and out of scope areas.

• A description of any trust assumptions.

• A description of various methodologies, techniques, tools (e.g. penetration testing, negative testing, internal or external validation, fuzz testing,…) to be used to validate the in scope areas.

• High level time line of when planned review areas/activities will be completed.

• An actionable list of test cases necessary to achieve the defined security and privacy coverage target. Click here for how to export the list of testing tasks in SD Elements.

• Trace-ability from security objectives to the security test cases.

• Tests that verify that the security configuration settings have been programmed correctly an actionable list of test cases necessary to achieve the defined security and privacy coverage target verification of input validation mechanisms

• Validation of any open source or 3rd party COTS APIs

• The timing of which test coverage will be executed in which timeframe (e.g. Alpha versus Beta, Pre-Si versus Post-Si…).

• Identification of what resources (internal and/or external) will be used to execute the validation plan. Depending on the size and complexity of the security/privacy validation effort, the validation lead may choose to review the plan with security experts, privacy experts, subject matter experts and stakeholders.

Confirm with functional validation team that product feature tests pass with the production security configuration settings enabled (i.e. functional validation must be performed with production security configuration settings). It is recommended that teams utilize an automation tool for checking the security configuration (example: Chipsec, COBRA).

Review Assigned Tasks and other Sources of Requirements SD Elements assigns a set of problems (or threats) and associated testing tasks for the project to address based on the responses to the survey. These problems are the basis for the threat model. For SW, the problems and tasks assigned by the tool may fully address all of the threats and validation needs for the project. It is possible, however, that there are additional threats and validation needs that were not discovered by the survey that require additional exploration. For FW and HW there will definitely be additional threats and validation needs that are not covered by the knowledgebase that will require additional security and privacy validation tasks.

 

Generate a Security/Privacy Validation Plan

If the set of testing tasks assigned to the project already addresses the relevant threats and security/privacy objectives, then the security/privacy validation plan is effectively complete. If, however, additional validation is needed then generate a Security/Privacy validation plan. The validation plan must include:

• A description of in scope and out of scope areas.

• A description of any trust assumptions.

• A description of various methodologies, techniques, tools (e.g. penetration testing, negative testing, internal or external validation, fuzz testing,…) to be used to validate the in scope areas.

• High level time line of when planned review areas/activities will be completed.

• An actionable list of test cases necessary to achieve the defined security and privacy coverage target. Click here for how to export the list of testing tasks in SD Elements.

• Trace-ability from security objectives to the security test cases.

• Tests that verify that the security configuration settings have been programmed correctly an actionable list of test cases necessary to achieve the defined security and privacy coverage target verification of input validation mechanisms

• Validation of any open source or 3rd party COTS APIs

• The timing of which test coverage will be executed in which timeframe (e.g. Alpha versus Beta, Pre-Si versus Post-Si…).

• Identification of what resources (internal and/or external) will be used to execute the validation plan. Depending on the size and complexity of the security/privacy validation effort, the validation lead may choose to review the plan with security experts, privacy experts, subject matter experts and stakeholders.

Confirm with functional validation team that product feature tests pass with the production security configuration settings enabled (i.e. functional validation must be performed with production security configuration settings). It is recommended that teams utilize an automation tool for checking the security configuration (example: Chipsec, COBRA). $acceptance criteria:$

Based on the list of test cases identified in SD Elements and/or the Security/Privacy validation plan, generate regression test cases and/or scripts. • The correctness of all control logic that protect the asset

• That protection control logic is used for every access to the asset

• That trusted inputs to the control logic are also protected

Security Validation MUST test security configuration of production builds/ product before final release to check security configuration settings are programmed as defined in security configuration spec.

Update Product security configuration specification to include any changes in requirements or new settings defined for bug fixes / workarounds or feature changes.

• Security assumptions made about the dependencies which are out of scope of this validation effort.

• What vulnerabilities would exist if the dependency fails to meet the trust assumption

• The owner for validating the dependency

Review security verification results and trust assumptions with appropriate owner. Incorporate recommendations into the execution plans. description:

 Use the following guidelines for verifying server-to-server authentication: Obtain a list of all servers in-scope for this application along with IP addresses.

description:

Use the following guidelines for testing that confidential data is not stored on a client, or in shared locations on a server, in an unencrypted format:

For client applications: Install the application on a client, such as a mobile device.

• If the device is protected, root or jailbreak the device, or use an emulator that simulates this. Locate the data-files and local databases, and then copy them. • It is usually possible to do so on rooted mobile devices through a USB cable.

• For mobile devices, check the data storage folders belonging to the application on the shared storage as well.

Inspect the contents of the files and the databases. This test fails if sensitive data such as application secrets or sensitive user data is stored without encryption.

For server applications:

Browse and analyze the directory structure on the server.

Inspect the contents of the files and the databases.

This test fails if sensitive data such as application secrets or sensitive user data is stored without encryption.

Test serialized objects

Locate the folders that hold application data especially 'serialized objects' (consult the developers). Check the content of those files/streams to test that confidential data is not stored in serialized objects without encryption.

summary: Pool create destroy transition to control plane Part 1
description:
h3. Problem
Currently, all the functional tests use DAOS API, which is in {{utils/py/daos_api.py}}, to create and destroy pool. However, the API isn't used by the end user, so testing the pool with DAOS API doesn't cover the end-to-end use cases.

h3. Solution
{{daos_shell}} is the control plane tool used by the end user, so we would like to use it in our tests instead of the API.

h3. High level processes:
We have recently added a wrapper around the API. The wrapper class is {{TestPool}} which is in {{util/test_utils.py}}. The first step is to update create and destroy functions in this class so that it uses {{daos_shell}} instead of the API. In order to use {{daos_shell}} from the test, we'll use {{DmgCommand}} class. This class already implements the {{storage}} subcommand of {{daos_shell}}, so we'll follow the pattern and add the {{pool}} subcommand.

Probably the bigger challenge is that there are many tests that directly use the API to create and destroy pool, so we need to modify those tests to use {{TestPool}}.

h3. Tasks for this ticket
Implement {{pool_create}} and {{pool_destroy}} functions in {{dmg_utils.py}}. Test those functions with a sample test to verify the functionalities.

h3. Note
* We might support other pool-related subcommands such as evict, exclude, add, remove, kill, query, so we should keep this in mind when we implement.
* {{daos_shell}} will be renamed to {{dmg}} in the near future.

summary: Test Automation: Basic aggregation test for overwritten data.
description:

Environment:
Run this test with a medium configuration 8 clients, 2 servers.

* Create a pool, container that spans the 2 servers.
* Run an IOR job that writes data for a number of minutes to the container.
* Check the utilized capacity for the container/pool.
* Run the IOR job a second time using the option for "same file" which causes it to overwrite existing logical locations.
* Watch the DAOS logs looking for aggregation to start and finish.
* Check the utilized capacity of the container/pool.  It should be roughly the same as after the initial run since aggregation has reclaimed the overwritten capacity.

summary: System level test for network interface detection (manual cfg)
description:
This feature was to be completed for 0.8 release (DAOS-2690 and DAOS-2691).

There is currently 'go' unit test in DAOS.

To run 'go' unit tests manually:

cd src/control

./run_go_tests.sh

This feature is made available via the daos_server app and can used in the following ways:
 * daos_server network scan –a
 * daos_server network list

The daos_server functionality above will be made available through daos_shell in future and will look like the following (but please check with daos_shell owner to verify when this gets implemented in daos_shell):

#daos_shell -i --debug network list

#daos_shell -i --debug network scan

 

The task in this ticket is to write a system level test that would test 
 * daos_server network scan –a
 * daos_server network list

and make sure the info returned is as expected on the test node. 

 

Addtional test suggestions is below and it's ok to create a separate ticket on these when worked on:

To further stress the testing, perhaps we could modify hwloc xml OR create a test version of ofi library with mocked fi_info, and see if  daos_server does indeed return the modified info. This will require understanding of working with hwloc and/or ofi, and have not been tried whether or not it will in VMs.

Or perhaps we could also test this on hw (for example with and without IB devices) and make sure the returned scan matches the expected output.

summary: Control plane tests need to be reorganized
description:
As the control plane is being reorganized into separate layers of functionality, the tests should also be updated. Current efforts have focused on modifying existing tests to work with the new organization, on the theory that we don't want to lose coverage.

It probably makes sense to step back and look at the existing tests and evaluate which aren't really adding value any more and which should be refactored to isolate their testing the the appropriate layer(s).

There isn't a hard rule that can be applied across the board... Generally speaking I think that integration tests add most value vs tons of small unit tests. However, as an example, we shouldn't have to set up a mock RPC layer in order to test the code which is responsible for probing and formatting SCM.

summary: Update ioserver to support SPDK primary mode (implementation)
description:
[~accountid:60357eab21d9bc00684ac647]: I'm going to put this on your plate for 0.9 for now. This task involves some modifications to the ioserver in order to fully support multiple i/o servers on a node. You may want to break this into research/implementation phases if that makes more sense. The basic idea is that we want to move the SPDK initialization into daos_io_server so that each instance is its own SPDK primary process, rather than having daos_server be a single primary process.

I think that there will be some work on the daos_server side to supply per-ioserver configuration details (nvme device lists, hugepage info, etc) to the instances. One thought was to leverage the nvme.conf generated by daos_server and written to the SCM mountpoint -- not sure if that is feasible.

summary: Add system (re)start subcommand
description:
Add ability to (re)start after shutdown. in order to have the CP keep running when instances stop and start we should be sending gRPC requests from the leader to the member hosts to have the host harnesses manage the start and stop of the instances (which may involve dRPC requests under the hood).

During controlled shutdown, members will transition from Started->Stopping->Stopped (with alternate states Errored/Unresponsive/Disabled) triggered by "prep" and "kill" phases respectively.

Restart will trigger the access point to start harness on all hosts (identified by reply address of member) listed in the membership that are in the "Stopped" state.

summary: Provide special handling for device name for PSM2 provider
description:
The libfabric PSM2 provider does not behave like the other providers in that it does not provide a fabric interface device names.  Rather than provide a name, such as hfi1_0, it provides an integer value in the fi_info record that can instead be used to implicitly determine the device name as "hfi_<n>"

Currently, the provider validation routine that is now part of the control plane, cannot validate the PSM2 provider / device combination without this proposed work around.

summary: Test ACL access when user/group management isn't synced between client and server nodes
description:
Based on requirement CR-111 from the v1.0 technical requirements: [https://wiki.hpdd.intel.com/display/DAOS/v1.0+Technical+Requirements]

*(CR-111) DAOS ACL still works if user/group management on the servers are not synchronized with compute nodes.*

Need a system-level test to verify this requirement is satisfied.

Basic test structure:
 * Set up compute node and server node with different system users/groups.
 * Create a pool with an ACL granting access to user on compute node.
 * Verify client user that was granted permissions can connect to the pool.

Suggested scenarios:
 * User exists on client but not server. ACL grants permissions to the specific user.
 * User is in group on client, and on server the user exists but is not in the group. ACL grants permissions to the group but not the user.

summary: Manual install following documented instructions on Centos 7.7
description:
Following the instructions found in the admin guide to install DAOS from scratch from RPMs. 

Environment:
1 server and 4 clients, server has SSDs and AEP.

Test Steps:
* Verify that admin guide clearly/correctly identifies SW prerequisites that must be in place prior to installing DAOS and perform those steps on the test configuration.
* Verify that the admin guide documents other prerequisites such as time synchronization and perform those steps on the test configuration.
* Verify that the admin guide documents security prerequisites such as certificate generation and perform those steps on the test configuration.
* Verify that the admin guide documents the server config file options and create a config file following that documentation
* Use the admin guide instructions to setup the small DAOS config defined above using the Centos 7.7 RPMs.  
* Verify that the RPM enforces documented prerequisites.
* Verify that setuid permission set on appropriate executables.  Verify that configuration steps can be completed with a regular user account.
*  Use DMG to create a pool to verify everything is functional.
*  Verify that every installed binary reports the correct version number (what should this be?)

summary: Test adding a new server to a DAOS cluster
description:
Test adding a new server to a DAOS cluster.

Environment:
Use a large DAOS cluster but a smaller number of clients, e.g. 8 DAOS servers, 1 client.

Test Steps:
* Start 6 of the 8 DAOS servers, create a pool across all of the 6 servers.
* Use the command line tool to list DAOS servers, expect to see the 6 that are running
* Start a 7th DAOS server.
* Use the command line tool to list DAOS servers, expect to see that 7 are now running
* Create a pool on the 7th server
* Perform operations  (e.g. connect and create a container) on both the 1st pool spanning 6 servers and the 2nd pool spanning a single server 
* Start the 8th DAOS server.
* Create a pool on the 8th server.
* Perform operations as above on all 3 pools
* Delete all three pools.
* Create a pool across all 8 servers.
* Perform operations as above on the pool

NOTE just an example set of steps, change as needed.
h3. 1.2 Test Step
This ticket and DAOS-3598 are similar, so I have reorganized the test steps. At a high level, this ticket covers the case of creating pools on single/multiple hosts where the hosts can be the ones that were started originally or ones later added to the system. Pool creation should work in all cases.
# Start 2 servers.
# Create 1 pool over one of the servers and another one across the 2 servers. To create a pool on the first host, use --ranks=0. To create on second host, use --ranks=1, and so on. To create a pool across all host, don't use --ranks.
# List the pools and verify. There should be 2. Also verify that the UUID named directories are created in /mnt/daos. Do both positive and negative testing, so check that pool 1 exists in rank0, pool 1 doesn't exit in rank1, and pool2 exist in both. Note that there's no mapping between rank and host, but it looks like rank0 is always the access point, rank1 is the other host, and rank2 will be the newly joined host in the next step, so we'll use this assumption. - Pool over partial and all hosts.
# Start a new server and join the system.
# Create 1 pool on the new server. List the pools; now there should be 3 pools. Also verify the UUID named directory in /mnt/daos for this new pool. - Pool on the new server.
# Create 1 pool across all servers. List the pools; now there should be 4 pools. Also verify the UUID named directory in /mnt/daos. - Pool across old and new servers.

summary: Test Automation: Verify pool create performance
description:
Verify pool create performance.

Environment: 
Use 8 servers and 1 client.  Servers have a full compliment of NVDIMMs (12)  & SSDs (4).

Test Steps:
* Setup DAOS servers according to admin guidelines, all storage devices should be freshly formatted and integrated into the DAOS server config.
* Create a single pool that utilizes all the PM on all the servers.  Verify that creating this pool takes no longer than 2 mins.
* Delete the pool
* Create a single pool that utilizes all the PM and all the SSD capacity in all of the servers.  Note that pool creation takes less than 4 mins.
* Delete the pool.
* On the 8 DAOS servers, create 3 pools per SSD (8 * 4 * 3 = 96) 
* Perform an orderly system shutdown via cmd line.
* Restart DAOS via cmd line tool, verify that DAOS is ready to accept requests within 2 minutes.

summary: (CR-52) status of the system can be retrieved to find out whether any io_server have crashed
description:
During "dmg system query", fanout to all the "Started"|"Unresponsive" members and send a gRPC "Status"/dRPC "PingRank" request.

If request times out, mark member as "Unresponsive".

If request succeeds, previously unresponsive, remains as unresponsive (as we are not in charge of eviction and currently don't have any way of being alerted about evictions in the control plane).

Measure of responsiveness is that the dRPC handlers inside the mgmt module of the IO Server are getting serviced in a timely manner. More logic to be added subsequently to Ping Rank dRPC handler to verify health of the IO server in more detail.

 

Work requires some reworking of the way membership is maintained in order to provide this feature in a reliable way.

 * add helper methods to system/member.go
 * unit tests for system/member.go
 * add helper methods to server/ctl_harness.go
 * unit tests for server/ctl_harness.go
 * ping rank drpc handler
 * unit tests for above handler
 * ping rank proto changes
 * ping rank drpc caller
 * unit tests for above caller
 * PingRanks|PrepShutdownRanks|KillRanks|StartRanks handlers that will perform dRPC requests to all ranks on a host
 * add unit tests for above handlers
 * fanout methods that aggregate results from all harnesses and update membership as necessary
 * add unit tests for fanout methods

summary: DMG usability verification
description:
dmg output is reasonable given up to 32 DAOS servers and typical associated hardware.

I did some research about the amount of output of each subcommands.
h3. Application Options

json: If --json is used, the output would be in json format. However, all the output would be in one message field of one line, so it doesn't make any improvement in terms of string parsing.
h3. network
list: 2 lines per host.
scan: 3 lines for each NIC. If there are 5 NICs per host and there are 2 hosts, then about 3*5*2=30 lines
h3. pool
create: 1 line regardless of the number of hardware
destroy: 1 line regardless of the number of hardware
list: Depends on the number of pools, not hardware
query: 10 lines regardless of the number of hardware
set-prop: 1 line per host, plus it supports brackets, so it doesn't get too long

h3. storage
query blobstore-health: 17 lines, fixed
query device-state: 5 lines, fixed
query nvme-health: 15 lines per NVMe device
query smd: 3 lines per NVMe device
format: 1 line per host (plus table's top row)
scan: 1 line per host

h3. system
list-pools: Depends on the number of pools, not hardware
query: 1 line per host, plus it supports brackets, so it doesn't get too long
leader-query: 2 lines regardless of the hardware

Overall, I believe we can support large number of hardware since we allow the user to select the host and we support the shortened hosts with brackets. The only concern is the JSON output. It doesn't really take advantage of JSON if we store almost the entire stdout to one message field.

For automation, I think it's reasonable to create a test that checks the number of lines in storage query commands. For nvme-health and smd, check the number of NVMe devices and verify the total number of lines.

 * Add ACL file that includes only new principals. The new principals should be added, leaving the rest of the list undisturbed.
